KEY MESSAGE 1...
A renewed push of moisture with long moisture transport vectors on 
morning mesoanalysis is ongoing this morning in strengthening 
southwest flow. Later this afternoon, a shortwave riding up the Ohio 
Valley will cross our region and enhance support for lift. Our 12z 
sounding showed a 1.54" PWAT values, though upstream at Wilmington, 
theirs was 2", and latest ACARS soundings from CMH and PIT are 
showing increasing deep layer moisture with eventual 99th percentile 
values by this afternoon areawide. With initial high clouds 
providing only modest hindrance to heating, no capping of note on 
model soundings, and increasing support for lift from warm advection 
and the approaching wave, CAMs suggest that scattered showers and 
thunderstorms begin to fire during the late morning and early 
afternoon hours. The environment will already be supportive of warm 
rain processes at that point given the increasing PWAT, increasingly 
saturated column, and deepening warm cloud depths.

As the afternoon wears on, these factors continue to improve, and a 
more robust shield of rain and embedded thunderstorms is likely as 
the shortwave approaches. Areas east of Pittsburgh may see enhanced 
low-level convergence as strengthening south/southwest flow butts up 
against southeast flow just to our east as surface high pressure 
moves farther away from the New England coast. This could locally 
enhance rainfall rates to concerning levels capable of flash 
flooding. HREF probabilities of greater than 1" are very high at 70-
95% from Pittsburgh south and east, greater than 2" at 60-80% east 
of Pittsburgh, and greater than 3" at 40-50%. LPPM values still 
reach up to 5-6". Such totals represent the high-end scenario, but 
the environment is certainly capable of supporting them. Much of the 
CWA has soil moisture levels in excess of 50% according to MRMS. 
Although low-level forcing may not be as robust as areas to the 
east, the same favorable environmental parameters for heavy rain 
(high PWAT/saturated soundings/etc) are present, and at least 
isolated flooding issues are possible. WPC has expanded the Slight 
Risk for excessive rainfall to virtually all of the forecast area. 
The Flood Watch remains in effect for the entire area through 
tonight.

In addition to the flooding threat, a window for strong to isolated 
severe thunderstorms exists. Joint 10km neighborhood probabilities 
of 1000 J/kg of SBCAPE and 30 knots of 0-6km shear reach 70-90% 
across much of the area this afternoon. While mid-level lapse rates 
will be poor given the deep saturation, and soundings eventually 
lead to tall and skinny CAPE profiles, there may be enough storm 
organization and steep low-level lapse rates to produce damaging 
wind potential with small-scale bowing structures possible. Even a 
tornado cannot be totally ruled out primarily east of Pittsburgh 
where locally backed low-level flow elongates hodographs a touch. ML 
guidance pegs a low-end tornado and wind threat today.

The heavy rain threat should begin to wane during the late 
evening/midnight period as the shortwave crosses, leaving some 
scattered showers in its wake. Lingering low-level moisture should 
lead to abundant stratus coverage by Sunday morning.

KEY MESSAGE 2...
Another severe weather threat could emerge on Sunday as 
developing Great Lakes troughing drops a surface cold front into
our region during the late afternoon and evening hours. The 
trough will provide sufficient deep shear on the order of 35-45 
knots, with higher values closer to the lakes. Moisture 
certainly remains present with surface dewpoints remaining in 
the upper 60s to around 70. However, there remains some question
as to the level of clearing and thus destabilization that can 
take place, as ensembles continue to suggest a range of sky 
cover outcomes. This results in 25th/75th percentile SBCAPE 
spreads of below 800 J/kg to above 1200 J/kg. Perhaps more 
inhibitive is a subsident warm layer around 800 mb that was 
evident in Friday's CAM runs and is even more prevalent across 
today's suite. In fact, a couple warm layers are showing up in 
model soundings. The RRFS was the only model that had been less 
capped, but even now the latest run is jumping ship and erring 
more toward the rest of the solutions. So, confidence in 
organized severe weather on Sunday is decreasing. Some CAMs do 
show at least widely scattered storm coverage during frontal 
passage, and given the shear, any storm will be capable of 
marginally severe wind and hail threats provided the warm layers
can be overcome. A more widespread threat could emerge if later
runs show better potential for destabilization and a lack of 
capping.

KEY MESSAGE 3... 
Minor timing issues remain, but ensembles have clustered into some 
better agreement that the trough axis crosses the region early 
Monday and maintains showers through the early morning hours before 
mid-level ridging provides a dry interlude by Monday afte
